vignette:
Eleanor sits in the chair opposite my desk with the ramrod straight posture of a woman who has spent fifty years commanding a courtroom. At 78, she still possesses the sharp, analytical gaze that I imagine has unsettled many a witness. She is here at the insistence of her husband, Robert, a fact she made clear with a wry, almost apologetic smile in our first session. She is a public defender, one of the old guard, and she speaks of her clients with a fierce, unsentimental protectiveness. She is not, she seems to imply, the kind of person who needs help.

Her story, as it has unfolded over the past few weeks, begins eight months ago on a Tuesday. It was an unseasonably warm evening in October, and she and Robert were taking their usual post-dinner walk around their quiet, tree-lined neighborhood. It was a ritual they had honored for decades, a time to decompress and discuss their days. Eleanor was recounting a frustrating cross-examination when two young men stepped out from behind a row of hedges. It happened with a speed that still leaves her breathless. One of them grabbed Robert, while the other pressed something cold and metallic against her temple.

She remembers the details with the chilling clarity of a legal affidavit. The scent of stale cigarette smoke on his jacket. The glint of the streetlamp on the cheap watch he wore. The rough, panicked quality of his voice as he demanded her purse and Robert's wallet. She, a woman who had faced down hostile judges and convicted felons without flinching, felt a profound and terrifying helplessness. The entire event lasted less than a minute. They shoved her to the ground before disappearing into the darkness. The physical injuries were minor-a scraped palm, a bruised hip-but as she lay on the cold pavement, looking up at Robert's terrified face, she felt a fundamental shift in the world she knew.

In the immediate aftermath, she handled it like a case. She gave a precise, detailed statement to the police, her voice steady. She declined the paramedics' offer to take her to the hospital. At home, she insisted she was fine, just shaken. For the first few weeks, she threw herself into her work, finding a familiar sense of control in the structured chaos of the courthouse.

But the armor began to crack. The evening walks stopped immediately; the thought of being outside after dusk now fills her with a low, humming dread. Before bed, she now performs a ritual that Robert pretends not to notice: checking the lock on the front door, then the back, then the front again, her hand pressing firmly against the wood as if to will it to be stronger. Sleep, when it comes, is shallow and frequently interrupted by jolting images of a dark street and a glint of metal.

Triggers are everywhere. The jingle of keys behind her in a parking garage can make her heart pound in her chest. Last month, a young client in a holding cell made a sudden move, and for a split second, she was back on the pavement, the same surge of adrenaline and terror flooding her system. She felt a wave of nausea and had to excuse herself, something she hasn't done in her entire career. She feels a deep, corrosive shame about this, a sense that she, of all people, should have been smarter, more aware. This self-blame has created a chasm between her and Robert. He sees her as a victim who needs comfort; she sees herself as a fool who failed to assess a threat. His attempts to console her feel patronizing, and she pushes him away, retreating into a stony silence. The easy intimacy they shared for fifty-two years has been replaced by a careful, fragile distance. She still goes to work every day, her formidable reputation preceding her, but she feels like an imposter, a defender of others who could not even defend herself.
